title: Aggregates, repositories and events
idea: DDD's building blocks for one model: an aggregate guards its rules through one root, a repository loads and saves whole aggregates, and domain events record what happened.
points: Callers go through the root, which checks each invariant (a rule that always holds).
A domain event is a past-tense fact, like `LineAdded`, that the root records.
A repository stores and loads whole aggregates, like an in-memory collection.
A domain service holds a rule that spans several aggregates.

code.title: Aggregate and repository
code.caption: Change the limit to 120 and run again. The lamp is accepted, and two events appear.

walk.text: `Order` is the root. Lines and events are private, so no one bypasses it.
The invariant is checked first; the line and its event are recorded only if it holds.
`pullEvents` hands over the recorded events once and clears them.
The repository stores whole orders by id. A real one would use a database.
The second line would pass the limit, so the root refuses it.
Save, then read the state and drain the events.

code.title: A domain service
code.caption: `transfer` touches two wallets, so it lives outside both.

walk.text: The rule spans two aggregates, so a stateless domain service owns it.
The second transfer fails, and the debit is refused before any credit.

pitfalls: Never return an aggregate's inner arrays; callers could bypass the invariant.
Keep aggregates small; a huge one makes unrelated writes block or overwrite each other.
Reference other aggregates by id, not by holding the object.

quiz.q: Which design keeps an order's "total at most 100" rule safe?
options: Expose `order.lines` so services can push lines directly
Let the repository check the total when saving
Route every change through `order.addLine`, which checks the limit
quiz.why: The root is the only way in, so it sees every change and can reject one that breaks the invariant.

takeaway: Change an aggregate only through its root, and save it whole.
